summary: An FBI memo on Ernest Hemingway's recruitment for American Embassy intelligence in Havana, 1942. Hemingway had friendly ties with Consul Kennet and Second Secretary Robert Joyce. The Ambassador, who coordinates intelligence, wanted Hemingway's wartime experience and Spanish Republican contacts used. Hemingway was to work directly with Joyce, not the writer, because of his 1940 Detroit neutrality-case criticism of the Bureau and a 'Gestapo' joke. From September 1942 he ran Spanish Republican informants, including four full-time and fourteen part-time, at about $500 a month, reporting on the Falange. His reports were dictated and well prepared.

nodes.summary: An FBI-related memo about Ernest Hemingway's 1942 intelligence work for the American Embassy in Havana. It covers the Ambassador's suggestion to clarify Hemingway's relationship with the Bureau, citing his 1940 signing of a criticism of the Bureau in the Detroit case and a Jai Alai incident where he introduced an agent as Gestapo. Joyce found Hemingway cooperative and decided he would work directly with Joyce, with Embassy special funds paying expenses. Hemingway began operations in September 1942 through Spanish Republican agents, costing about $500 monthly, and reports to Joyce. The Ambassador favored his approach, and Hemingway declined a $150,000 Hollywood script offer.

nodes.summary: An October 9, 1942 Havana Legal Attache letter to the FBI Director reports on Ernest Hemingway's arrangement with the Naval Attache to conduct coastal patrol and intelligence work off Cuba's south coast. Hemingway, a known fisherman with marlin-migration research ties to a New York museum, received patrol permits, gasoline, and requested firearms and depth charges, with crew promised war-casualty indemnification. He investigates Spanish Falange activity and German suspects, reports promptly, works without compensation, and has caused no conflict with Bureau work in Havana. The writer promises ongoing updates and requests guidance.

nodes.title: Dear Sir:
nodes.summary: A 1942 FBI-filed letter from the Legal Attaché in Cuba reports that Gustavo Duran is being sent from Washington to assist Ernest Hemingway in intelligence work under Embassy auspices, citing Duran's prior Spanish Civil War intelligence service. It notes Mrs. Hemingway's October 1942 Washington visit as Mrs. Roosevelt's guest, used to brief the Roosevelts on Cuban intelligence and a stalled request to fund internment and investigation. It also records a request for $1 million for Cuban authorities, and the Ambassador's concern about involving Berle, with a closing comment on the Bureau's non-involvement and a signature by Hendon Kramer.

His October 1942 coastal patrol arrangement with the Naval Attache is described, including requested weapons, crew indemnification, and Falange investigations. Gustavo Duran was sent to assist him, and Mrs. Hemingway's Washington visit and a $1 million funding request are noted.

title: MEMORANDUM FOR THE DIRECTOR
summary: An FBI memorandum for the Director, referencing Attaché R.G. Leddy in Havana, reports that Ernest Hemingway, residing near Havana, served as an informant for Ambassador Braden. Hemingway supported the Spanish Republic, opposed the Bureau in 1940 over the Detroit arrests, and was accused of Communist sympathies, which he denies. He runs informants among Spanish refugees, and his reports are considered valueless and unfounded, wasting Bureau investigative effort. Leddy has not objected to the arrangement, and suggests the Bureau raise it with Braden. The memo notes Hemingway's probing of Cuban officials and police chief Walden risks embarrassment and trouble for the Bureau, and that Gustavo Duran assists him.

The memo recommends Agent Leddy persuade the Ambassador to fully end Hemingway's informant services, since Hemingway was branching into an uncontrolled investigative organization; the Bureau should not protest at the Seat of Government first, to preserve the Ambassador's confidence in Leddy and other agents. The letter to the FBI Director in Washington reports that the Ambassador's Embassy official confidentially said Hemingway's Cuban intelligence organization was disbanded effective April 1, 1943 without notice to the FBI, and that a full report on its activities will follow.

summary: An FBI document (c. 1942-1943, Director J. Edgar Hoover) on Ernest Hemingway's unofficial intelligence work in Cuba. The memo flags unreliable information transmitted without official checks, and the Bureau's wish to protect confidential sources. nodes.summary: A circular and New York Times notice (May 1937) announced Ernest Hemingway as a speaker at the American Writers Congress at Carnegie Hall, alongside Earl Browder, Archibald MacLeish and others; a confidential source said he was close to the Communist Party. A 1941 New York World-Telegram article by Frederick Woltman called the Fourth Writers Congress a Communist cultural front, listing Hemingway among those who resigned. Hemingway was a vice-president and board member of the League of American Writers (reported 1941) and was named president of its National Board in a circular soliciting funds for Spanish Loyalist exiles stranded in France. Letters from 1942 expected the Hemingways in Mexico, and a March 1942 informant said he lived at the Hotel Reforma under an assumed name and spent much time with German Communist author Gustav Regler.

summary: An FBI Legal Attache memo on Hemingway's reports from Cuba (1942-43). Hemingway's reports were unverified, like voluntary complaints, with no continuing investigation. The "Voice of the Street" public-opinion reports sampled only cafe/bar patrons and were not representative, though the Ambassador valued them. Hemingway alleged an oxygen/submarine-supply plot, which was found well-accounted for. He also alleged a police-chief coup plot by General Benites, which was unfounded, and that Ruspoli bribed police to fake illness, which was never followed up.

summary: An FBI memorandum excerpt (Page 5) on Hemingway's Cuban investigations: he claimed a submarine refueling breakthrough, but oxygen tank checks showed well-accounted supplies and nothing further came of it. He then alleged General Benites planned to seize power during Batista's absence, citing police rifle training and motorcycle squads; the Legal Attache found no such preparations, noting police training with rifles is longstanding and warning that such reports risk alienating police cooperation. Hemingway also claimed Prince Camilo Ruspoli bribed Police Chief Benites and was not really ill; he promised health details via an undercover nurse but nothing followed.

summary: An FBI memorandum (Ladd, Legal Attaché Leddy, Havana) on Ernest Hemingway's undercover activities in Cuba, 1942-43. It covers his unverified report of Prince Ruspoli at a luncheon; his claimed submarine sighting near a Spanish steamer, which investigation found baseless; the January 1943 box episode at Bar Basque (only a cheap book was found); and his February 1943 charges against Agent Knoblaugh. It also covers the Ambassador ending the operation's paid informants while keeping public-opinion reports; Hemingway's hostility toward the FBI, influence, and vindictiveness; and a recommendation for discretion. A handwritten addendum disagrees with that recommendation, and a further note defends Leddy.

nodes.summary: The text describes Gustavo Duran, a Spanish musician and member of Madrid's young intelligentsia before 1936, well known in musical and artistic circles. At the outbreak of the Spanish Civil War in July 1936 he joined the Republican forces despite no prior military experience and rose rapidly. After field service near Madrid, he moved to the Valencia front in 1938 and became commander of an Army Corps as a Lieutenant Colonel. He was a vigorous, stern disciplinarian who tolerated no misconduct by soldiers.

nodes.summary: Describes Gustavo Duran, a Republican army officer whose disciplined corps behaved well and who was respected by his soldiers. His rapid rise was due to favor with the Communist Party, which he may have belonged to, giving him influence in the Army and with civilian officials. Since arriving in Habana he has avoided former friends and Communists, keeping limited ties to Spanish refugees, and his current sentiments are unknown. The source, a Cuban-born Republican opposed to Franco since 1936 and not pro-Communist, is noted as reliable. An informal interview with Duran was held to check these statements.

nodes.summary: Memo of SIS #498 (July 30, 1945) recounting an interview with Duran on Communist strength in Spain. Duran says the Spanish Communist Party had about 30,000 members, roughly half actual members and half sympathizers. Many Republicans joined to serve the cause because Russia was the only aid source and required Communist pilots and materials. Russian equipment was obsolete, e.g., 1905 artillery, which cooled enthusiasm. Many dropped membership after defeat. Duran was in Madrid last in June 1938, then commanded the Valencia sector until war's end; Miaja is mentioned.

Proposed checks include interviewing Col. Casado, contacting Spanish exiles in Mexico, reviewing MID records, and searching Loyalist-era publications. Part two is a letter from the Havana legal attaché about Ernest Hemingway's book on his Cuban intelligence work, which portrays FBI agents unfavorably.

nodes.summary: An OCR-garbled 1943 FBI memorandum (Bureau file, marked personal and confidential, sent by diplomatic air courier) about Ernest Hemingway's activities in Cuba. It notes Hemingway is writing a book on his intelligence experiences there under the American Ambassador, likely naming Ambassador Braden and others he dealt with. The Bureau legal attache in Havana has no information on whether FBI representatives will be mentioned. Hemingway's hostility toward the FBI is noted: he signed a 1940 petition criticizing the Bureau in the Detroit Spanish Enlistment case and called the FBI the 'American Gestapo.' An informant reports he called the FBI a mediocre intelligence organization. The memo also suggests the letter be destroyed once it has served its purpose.

nodes.summary: An FBI document about Gustavo Duran, an employee of the American Embassy in Havana. It covers Ernest Hemingway's intelligence work, which was discontinued in 1943 after charges against Special Agent Knoblaugh. It also covers Duran's ongoing public-opinion reports, his informants, his hostility toward FBI representatives, and reports linking him to Communist Party membership in Spain. Sources, a suggested Mexico City contact, and State Department records are also discussed.

nodes.title: RECOMMENDATIONS
nodes.summary: Recommendations on suspected Communist Party membership of Gustavo Duran, based on confidential informant reports from Cuba. Proposes further discreet inquiry: recontacting Bureau Legal Attache in Havana's sources (Spanish Republicans and anti-Communists) about reports Duran joined Communists fighting Republicans who favored surrendering Madrid to Franco. Suggests a blind memorandum to Mr. Berle and State Department requesting their files on Duran's activities in Spain and Europe. Advises Berle that Duran's Embassy presence in Havana would impair Bureau operations; notes Duran is a friend of Ernest Hemingway and Ambassador Spruille Braden.

summary: An FBI memorandum (Sept 1943, Washington D.C.) on Ernest Hemingway's unofficial intelligence work in Cuba. After April 1, 1943 the Ambassador ended his intelligence service, but he continued cruising Cuban waters in a small boat to look for submarines, reportedly with Naval Attache backing. Hemingway told an SIS representative he is writing a book on these experiences that will name Ambassador Braden and others he contacted. Hemingway's hostility to the Bureau is noted, including his petition against the FBI in the Detroit Spanish Enlistment case. A columnist's mention of his Cuba trip and a September 1943 Caribbean voyage with Winston are also recorded.

summary: An OCR-garbled FBI memo (c.1944, marked confidential) about Ernest Hemingway's intelligence activities in Cuba. It reports Hemingway has stopped writing on his intelligence work and is doing no writing now, though he considered three plots for books. Martha Gellhorn was in New York arranging publication of a book on Martinique, partly based on State Department information. Hemingway retains Ambassador Braden's confidence, and a gasoline charge from April 1943 suggests his arrangement continued. His assistant Gustavo Duran, allegedly a Communist, carries on part of the program. The Bureau plans agents at the Havana embassy to watch for any Hemingway book mentioning the Bureau. Hemingway praised Bureau representatives and his friend General Batista.

summary: The text is an OCR-garbled passage about Ernest Hemingway. In 1938 he reportedly contributed to "Among Friends," a quarterly published by the Friends of the Abraham Lincoln Brigade, devoted to the Loyalists in Spain and the Brigade. The Daily Worker (Feb 3, 1939) announced he would speak on Feb 22, 1939, at a memorial for ten Brigade members who died fighting. The Brigade's letterhead listed him as a sponsor in June 1939. The Attorney General later cited the Brigade as within Executive Order 9335.

It describes a January 1940 letter over Ernest Hemingway's signature endorsing the committee's work and soliciting help and contributions, a conference on protection of foreign-born persons held in Washington, and a sponsors' circular co-signed by committee co-chairmen. title: WR. FLETCHER
summary: An FBI memorandum (partly redacted, OCR-garbled) responding to an Office of the Secretary of Defense request for a file check on Ernest Hemingway, for security clearance purposes. It reports that Hemingway ran an intelligence operation for the American Ambassador in Havana, Cuba (Aug 1942 to Apr 1943) and had frequent contact with the Legal Attache there. The Legal Attache reported in June 1943 that Hemingway showed surface friendliness toward the FBI but privately held it in low esteem and was ideologically hostile to it, calling it the "American Gestapo." Hemingway was a principal signer of a 1940 denunciation of the FBI in the Detroit Communist-Spanish enlistment case; he later said he signed petitions casually as a favor and dismissed the "Gestapo" remark as a jest.

Scott showed a letter from Pessino quoting Hemingway's refusal, citing ill health and much writing, and saying a court of honor would not consider it cowardice. Scott was not satisfied. summary: An FBI memo dated August 26, 1954 from Havana, Cuba concerns Edvard 'Ted' Scott, a New Zealand-born British subject and Havana Post columnist, who was friendly with Ernest Hemingway. Scott's column quoted Hemingway's laudatory remarks, then reported a dispute with Mrs. Hemingway (Mary), who called him a 'stupid British colonial.' Scott also criticized actress Ava Gardner's abusive treatment of Cuban press and noted Frank Sinatra's feud with the press. The memo explains no local dissemination was made to protect an informant's position, and addresses Dr. Jacob Canter, a USIA representative linked by Senator Sprukle's testimony to alleged communist ties.

summary: An OCR-garbled 1964 letter packet from Quentin Reynolds to J. Edgar Hoover, dated January 6, 1964. Reynolds reports that Mary Hemingway is upset that a commemorative 'Primer Dia' stamp, mailed from Havana by Ernest Hemingway's part-time secretary Roberto Herrera, could imply Hemingway sympathized with Castro. Reynolds notes Hemingway owned a Cuban house, disliked Batista, and met Castro only briefly. Mary sold the house to the Cuban government in exchange for Hemingway's unfinished manuscripts. The family worries communists could exploit the stamp. Reynolds gives contact details for Mary and himself, offers condolences about Clyde, and asks that the envelope be returned to Mary if not needed. The text carries Hoover's office routing and a note that Reynolds is on the Special Correspondents' List.

summary: A January 14, 1974 letter from the University of Florida Libraries (Social Sciences Research Librarian) to the FBI Director in Washington. It responds to a December 11, 1973 letter to Professor James K. Lyon of the German Department. The FBI files on Bertolt Brecht can be obtained for $160, pending approval from Brecht's heirs. The letter asks whether the library can hold the material, whether the public can access it, and requests FBI files on Elizabeth Bentley, Whittaker Chambers, Ernest Hemingway, and John Dos Passos.

summary: An OCR-garbled letter from a federal Bureau to Mr. Ray Jones, Research Librarian at the University of Florida Libraries, about Dr. James K. Lyon's request for files on Bertolt Brecht. The Bureau has no objection to the documents becoming part of the library collection. Its indices show voluminous references on Elizabeth Bentley, Whittaker Chambers, Ernest Hemingway, and John Dos Passos that must be reviewed. Files total about 102,539 pages. Under 28 CFR 16.9 a fee applies: estimated $16,200, with a 25% deposit of $4,075 by check or money order to the Treasury, not a guarantee of full release. Routing and enclosure notations are also present.
